segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: I'm so pleased you've mentioned the Haynesville case, Jacques, because that was where I was going next. Let's talk about that, because I think it's a great illustration of the fact that you have this prodigious understanding because of the data you've been involved in collecting. Friday, December 30, 1966, Dr. Louie Galloway is traveling with his wife and two kids through a heavily forested area near Haynesville, Louisiana, close to the Arkansas border. Now, he's a professor of physics, which is really helpful for what actually happens. And they see a powerful pulsating luminous phenomenon in or behind the forest. It's initially red-orange, then its luminosity increases dramatically to an intense white brilliance, the light so bright that it overwhelms the car's headlights, illuminates the woods on both sides of the highway, and he shields his eyes in order to continue seeing the road. Now, what I love, and you've alluded to this a moment ago, is that the studies of what the light did to the forest environment — in a scientific paper referred to in 2025, I think you were involved in writing this — the paper estimated the radiative energy values at between approximately 500 and 1,400 megawatts. That's 0.5 to 1.4 GW of power, which is the approximate power range of a nuclear power station, in a luminous object just a few meters across, in a forest in Louisiana, and it's raining.

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: That case came to me because at the time I was working with Dr. Josef Allen Hynek, with a small contract with Project Blue Book to redo their statistics. They knew that their statistics were very amateurish and they wanted to have a computer system of statistics that I had proposed to develop for them. So I was paid something like $200 a month, and they were sending me the batches of current cases and I was going through them. Nothing was classified — there were a few classified things, because when it was a classified radar they had an interference or something like that, but most of the data was open, contrary to what people say now.

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: I find this one case, and I called Dr. Hynek and I said: the witness is a university professor, we should call him to get the details, and if it matches what he's describing, we should introduce him to Professor Edward U. Condon. Professor Condon was then in charge of a reassessment of the Air Force effort, Project Blue Book, and Professor Condon had been with Robert Oppenheimer at Trinity when the bomb went off. So we put them in touch, nuclear physics professor to nuclear physics professor, and Professor Condon redid the calculation and came up with the value of the energy twice what the witness had estimated. Now, for a long time I couldn't publish that paper, it sort of lingered in between, because the question was to pinpoint exactly where the object had been.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The case is listed as unidentified in the final report by the Condon report, which was a notorious cover-up, because Condon was caught out basically admitting that the whole thing was a setup in the first place and that he was operating under a brief to basically shut down the whole issue. But even Professor Edward Condon admitted that the source of this incredible energy remains unidentified. I love the symmetry, Jacques, that 60 years on from that classic case, you're the one that reminds us all that there are nuggets deep in the UFO databases which allow us to reach a conclusion about the validity of this phenomenon being highly anomalous, despite government secrecy. I guess that's the key message from the Haynesville case.

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: Yes. It went to the Academy of Sciences, and that report was published by the academy, and it contains that one-third of the cases they looked at were not explained. But people don't look at that, because people look at the conclusion, and the conclusion doesn't say that we shouldn't study that — he says people are free to study whatever they want, but he says that it's probably not the most important thing to fund as research. That led to the Air Force shutting down Project Blue Book. And I sympathize with their view: they want to fly airplanes, they don't want to go around in rainy woods at night trying to find if there was a flying saucer. That didn't make any sense.
